title: Legal pages that are still part of the brand
metaTitle: Legal pages that still feel like you
excerpt: Privacy and terms can be plain and still use your type and layout. A default template in a new window feels like a different company attached to yours.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table. The shared table fits a piece about legal pages that should still belong to the same team and the same site.
caption: The policy should look like the rest of the house. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a privacy policy match the rest of the site?
faqs.answer: Yes, in type, layout, and header. The content can be plainer than the homepage, and it should be. It should not look like a vendor's template opened in a new window. A reader who clicks Privacy is still on your site, judging whether you are the same company that just asked for their email.

faqs.question: Can design matter if a lawyer wrote the text?
faqs.answer: Design does not replace the text, and this is not legal advice. Design makes the text readable: real headings, a measure you can follow, links that work, a date, and a contact. Ask counsel to own the claims. Ask the studio to set those claims in the site's system so people can actually read them.

faqs.question: What should the page include besides the policy?
faqs.answer: A clear title, the date it was updated, a way to reach you, and headings that match the subjects a person came to check. Cookies, analytics, and contact details should use the same words as the banner and the forms. A policy that contradicts the banner is a trust problem the layout will not hide.

markdown:
Privacy and terms can be plain and still use the site's type and layout. That is the standard for privacy policy page design. A default template in a new window feels like a different company. The reader clicked a link in your footer because they wanted to know what you do with their name. Meet them in the same house.

This is a design problem sitting next to a legal one. The studio should not invent the legal claims. Counsel, or a tool your counsel accepts, should own the substance. The page should still be yours: readable, current, and visibly part of the site. A beautiful policy that says the wrong thing is a failure. An accurate policy that looks abandoned is a failure too.

## Same site, plain language

Use the real header and footer. The person should be able to get back to the offer, the work, or contact without hunting. Opening the policy in a new window, on a blank domain, with a different logo, tells them the promise lives somewhere else. Keep it on your domain, in your layout, at a normal URL.

Plain language is part of the brand, not a dumbing-down. Short sentences. Defined terms when you truly need them. Headings that say what the section covers. "Who we share data with" is a heading. "Miscellaneous" is a drawer. A reader with a specific worry should be able to find the section. They are often skimming because they are deciding whether to trust a form.

The W3C's WCAG 2 overview treats web content, including text, as something that should be perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A policy is web content. WCAG 2.2 is the version W3C encourages. Understandable, here, means a structure a person can follow and language that matches the rest of the site's honesty. You can be legally precise and still use the words you use everywhere else for the same ideas.

Do not set the policy as a PDF unless you have a strong reason and an HTML version beside it. PDFs break the header, the search, the resizing, and often the contrast. They feel like a file someone exported and stopped owning. HTML in the article column is the version you can maintain.

## Type and layout

Set the policy in the same text face as an article, in the same measure, with the same line height. A legal page is a long read. The typography advice for a long article applies directly. Display faces, tiny gray text, and a full-bleed line of 200 characters are all ways of saying you hope nobody reads this. Assume someone will.

Headings need levels, in order, so a person can jump. A wall of bold inline clauses is how templates try to look serious. It is hard to scan and hard to operate with a keyboard reader. Give each obligation or explanation a heading and a short paragraph. Lists are appropriate for the categories of data or the list of cookies. They are not appropriate as the entire visual style, a stack of bullets with no sentences.

Links inside the policy should look like links on the rest of the site, and they should go where they say. A link to "contact us" that 404s, or that points at a generic vendor, is a broken promise in the most literal page you publish. Check them when you check the footer. The footer is full of these URLs, and they rot first because nobody demos them.

Contrast and focus apply. A pale footer link that opens a pale policy fails twice. The focus ring on a long document is how a keyboard user moves. Do not strip it because the template's CSS reset did. Bring the policy into the same stylesheet as the marketing pages. A one-off "legal skin" will drift, and it will drift toward unreadability.

## The new window and the other brand

Watch for the seams. A cookie tool that hosts the policy. A payment provider's terms that you framed without saying so. A newsletter vendor's privacy page linked as if it were yours. Some of those links are necessary. Label them. "Payments are handled by X, and their terms are here" is honest. Presenting their page as your privacy policy is not.

If a vendor requires their clause, quote or link it inside your page rather than abandoning the visit. The reader should always know whose sentence they are reading. A change of type is a useful signal for a quoted clause, used sparingly. A change of entire website is a shove.

Avoid the double footer, yours and the template's, and the cookie banner that appears again on the policy page in a second style. The policy page is where you explain the banner. It should not be where a second banner argues with the first. One system, one set of words.

Print the page once. Not because you expect printing, but because print reveals whether the document stands on its own. A URL, a title, a date. If the printed page has no idea which company it belongs to, the HTML is leaning too hard on a header image. Put the name in the text.

## Dates, contact, and agreement with the product

Put the updated date where a person can see it, and change it when the text changes. Do not bump the date to look fresh. A date is a claim. Counsel and the person who edits the site should both know who is allowed to change it. An engineer "cleaning up" a template can accidentally publish a draft. Treat the policy like production code. Review it.

The contact has to work. An email you read, or a form that reaches a person, described the same way as on the contact page. If privacy requests go to a different place than sales, say so, and watch that inbox. A policy that names an address nobody opens is a process bug dressed as compliance.

Make the policy and the product agree. If the banner says analytics are optional, the policy should describe that choice and the tool by a name a person can recognize. If the form says you will only use the email to reply, the policy should not describe a marketing list you never mentioned. Alignment is the design task after the legal task. Read them side by side, out loud.

Terms of use, if you need them, get the same treatment. Same column, same type, a date, a contact. Do not mix terms and privacy into one unlabeled scroll. They answer different questions. A buyer looking for "do you sell my data" should not have to parse warranty disclaimers to find out. Separate pages, linked from the footer, with titles that say which is which.

## Cookies, forms, and the words that must match

List the cookies and similar storage you actually use, in the same names the banner uses. Necessary, measurement, marketing: if those are the labels on the button, those are the labels in the policy, with one sentence each about what they do here. A table copied from a platform that mentions products you do not run will be wrong on the day you publish it. Start from your tag list. Then write.

Forms should point at the policy in the same breath as the promise. Near the email field, a short line: what you will do with the address, and a link. The line and the policy section should be readable as a pair. If the form is only a reply, say reply. If you will add them to a list, say that before they submit, not only in a document they might never open.

When you add a tool, update the policy in the same release. A new chat widget, a new pixel, a new font host that sets a cookie: each one can change the true document. Put "update the policy" on the launch checklist next to "update the banner." The page is part of the product, and it drifts the moment the product does.

## A review that is not a legal review

Once counsel has signed off on the words, review the page as a page. Tab through it. Zoom the text. Read the headings only, and see if they form a map. Click every link. Open it on a phone. Confirm the cookie banner, if it shows, does not cover the heading you came to read.

Compare the voice to the homepage. You are not trying to make the policy charming. You are trying to make it sound like the same adults. If the homepage is plain and the policy is a thicket of unused clauses copied from a different business, ask counsel which clauses are actually yours. Cutting what does not apply is often their recommendation too. A shorter true policy is easier to design and easier to keep true.

Do not badge the page with a compliance logo you do not understand. A badge is a claim, like a client logo. If you cannot explain it, leave it off. The readable policy is the signal. The badge is decoration that can be wrong.

Put the policy URL in the places you promised it: the footer, the form near the submit button, the cookie banner. Each of those links should hit the same current page, not a cached PDF and not an old campaign URL. One canonical page is how you avoid contradicting yourself.

On a Hanabi site the legal pages live in the same system as the articles. Same header, same measure, headings you can scan. The founder brings the approved text. The build makes it a page a person can finish. That division of labor keeps both the law and the layout honest.

See [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) if the footer still dumps people onto a template you do not recognize. The work is to bring those pages into the site you are already proud to show.

A second language makes the same demand, twice. [Multilingual sites without a mess](/blog/multilingual-sites-without-a-mess) is the next piece, because a policy, an offer, and a nav only work when each language has a real page, not a toggle over an untranslated hole.
